title: Cost Accounting

pattern.summary: Usually 8 questions, answer any 5, each 20 marks — a mix of theory and sums (stores ledger, process accounts, contract accounts, operating costs, overheads, reconciliation).
pattern.note: The June 2023 to June 2024 papers had Section A (all compulsory, 40 marks) and Section B (any 3 of 5 sums, 20 marks each).

sessionNotes.2023-06: Section A (compulsory) + Section B (any 3). Scanned paper — text typed in by hand.

choosing: A stores ledger (FIFO or LIFO), process accounts and an operating cost sum come up in almost every paper — practise one of each.
Theory on purchasing, labour turnover and the objectives of cost accounting gives safe marks.
Pick sums you can finish; in costing, a correct format earns marks even with an arithmetic slip.
numerical: Show working notes and units beside amounts.
Use the standard formats: stores ledger columns, process account in T-form, operating cost sheet.
State the basis you use for every apportionment.

topics.name: Pricing of Material Issues (FIFO, LIFO)
topics.summary: Stores ledger under FIFO and LIFO, other pricing methods, returns and shortages, material cost from a supplier's invoice, problems in pricing issues.
points: FIFO: materials are issued at the price of the oldest lot in stock; closing stock is at the latest prices. In rising prices it shows lower cost and higher profit.
LIFO: issues at the price of the latest lot; closing stock at old prices; charges current prices to production. (Not allowed for financial statements under AS 2, but asked in cost accounts.)
Other methods: simple average, weighted average, standard price, replacement price.
Returns to supplier: taken out at their purchase price. Returns from production (materials received back): treated as a fresh receipt at the price they were issued, or reissued first.
Shortage found on verification: normal shortage is absorbed in the cost of good units; abnormal shortage is written off to costing profit and loss.

Material cost from an invoice: price less trade discount + freight, insurance, non-recoverable taxes and charges for returnable containers minus the credit expected for their return; cash discount is ignored (a financial item).
Problems in pricing issues: prices change between lots, a method has to be chosen, returns and shortages, many small lots, effect on stock value and profit.
mistakes: Pricing an issue from one lot when it needs units from two lots — split it.
method: Draw the stores ledger with receipt, issue and balance columns.
Enter the opening stock and each receipt as a separate lot with its rate.
For each issue, take units lot by lot — oldest first (FIFO) or latest first (LIFO) — and show each lot's quantity × rate.
Enter returns from production as a receipt at the original issue price; returns to supplier as an issue at purchase price.
Record shortages as an issue (normal) or separately (abnormal).
After every entry, show the balance lots and total value.
formula: Value of issue = Σ (units taken from each lot × that lot's rate)
topics.frame: Stores ledger with columns Receipts (qty, rate, amount) | Issues (qty, rate, amount) | Balance (qty, rate, amount).

topics.name: Process Costing & Equivalent Production
topics.summary: Process accounts, normal and abnormal loss and gain, scrap, and equivalent production statements.
points: Process costing: used where production passes through continuous processes (chemicals, textiles, oil, food); the output of one process is the input of the next.
Process account: debit — units introduced, materials, labour, direct expenses, overheads; credit — normal loss at scrap value, abnormal loss, output transferred to the next process.

Normal loss: expected and unavoidable; its scrap value is credited; the cost is carried by good units. Abnormal loss: loss beyond normal, valued like good units and charged to costing profit and loss. Abnormal gain: actual loss below normal.
Equivalent production: work in progress expressed as completed units for each element (materials, labour, overheads) using its percentage of completion.
Three statements: equivalent production, cost per equivalent unit, and evaluation of output and work in progress.
mistakes: Valuing abnormal loss at scrap value — it is valued at the cost per good unit.
method: Normal loss units = input × normal loss %; its value = units × scrap rate.
Cost per unit = (total cost − scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (input units − normal loss units).
Abnormal loss units = normal output − actual output (abnormal gain if negative).
Value output and abnormal loss at the cost per unit; transfer output to the next process.
In the abnormal loss account, credit its scrap value and take the balance to costing P&L.
For WIP: statement of equivalent production → cost per equivalent unit → evaluation.
formula: Cost per unit = (Total cost − Scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (Input − Normal loss units)
Equivalent units = Completed units + (WIP units × % complete)
topics.frame: Working table for normal loss and cost per unit → Process I account → Process II account → Abnormal loss/gain account.

topics.name: Labour Cost: Time Keeping, Wage Plans & Turnover
topics.summary: Time keeping and time booking, idle time and overtime, labour turnover — causes, measurement and control — and wage plans (time rate, Halsey, Rowan, Taylor).
points: Time keeping: recording attendance (arrival and departure) — attendance register, disc/token method, time-recording clock, biometric systems. It is the basis for paying wages.
Time booking: recording time spent on each job or process — job cards, daily or weekly time sheets. Purposes: charge labour cost to jobs, find idle time, check efficiency, overtime control.

Idle time: time paid for but not worked. Normal idle time (tea breaks, change of shift) is included in labour cost or overheads; abnormal idle time (power failure, strikes, machine breakdown) goes to costing profit and loss.
Overtime: work beyond normal hours; the premium is charged to the job if the customer asked for it, to overheads if normal, to costing P&L if abnormal.

Labour turnover: rate of change in the workforce. Causes — avoidable (low wages, poor conditions, bad relations, no promotion), unavoidable (retirement, death, illness, marriage, moving). Control — fair pay, good conditions, proper selection and training, promotion policy, grievance handling, exit interviews.

Wage plans: time rate; piece rate; Taylor's differential piece rate (a low rate below standard output, a high rate at or above it); Halsey premium plan (time wages + 50% of time saved × rate); Rowan plan (time wages + time saved ÷ time allowed × time taken × rate).
method: Standard output for the period = standard per hour × hours worked.
Taylor: compare each worker's output with standard and apply the low or high piece rate.
Halsey/Rowan: find time allowed, time taken and time saved, then apply the bonus formula.
Labour turnover: separations ÷ average number of workers × 100 (or replacements, or flux method).
formula: Halsey earnings = Time taken × Rate + 50% × Time saved × Rate
Rowan earnings = Time taken × Rate + (Time saved ÷ Time allowed) × Time taken × Rate
Labour turnover (separation) = Separations ÷ Average workers × 100
topics.frame: Meaning → methods or causes as headings → conclusion; for wage plans, show the calculation for each worker.

topics.name: Purchasing & Material Control
topics.summary: Steps in purchasing materials, purchase requisition and order, centralised and decentralised purchasing, and requirements and advantages of material control.
points: Purchase procedure: purchase requisition from stores or department → finding suppliers (enquiries, quotations, tenders) → selecting the supplier → purchase order → follow-up → receiving and inspection (goods received note) → checking the invoice against order and GRN → passing for payment → records.

Purchase requisition: a request to the purchase department to buy materials — item, quantity, date needed, signed by an authorised person. Purchase order: the written order to the supplier — item, quantity, price, terms, delivery.
Centralised purchasing: one department buys for all. Advantages — bulk discounts, specialist buyers, uniform policy, better control; disadvantages — delays, higher overhead, may not suit local needs.
Decentralised purchasing: each unit buys for itself. Advantages — quick, flexible, local suppliers; disadvantages — no bulk discounts, duplication, weaker control.

Material control: making sure the right materials are available at the right time at minimum cost. Requirements: proper purchase procedure, receiving and inspection, good storage, issues against requisitions, perpetual inventory, stock levels, classification and codes, ABC analysis, internal checks.
Advantages: no stock-outs or overstocking, less waste and theft, lower investment in stock, accurate material costs.
topics.frame: Steps as a flow chart or headings → advantages → conclusion.

topics.name: Contract & Job Costing
topics.summary: Contract accounts, notional profit, profit on incomplete contracts, work-in-progress, contractee's account, and job vs contract costing.
points: Contract costing: used for large, long-duration work at a site (buildings, bridges); each contract is a cost unit. Job costing: for small, short jobs done to order in the factory (printing, repairs). Differences: size, duration, place, cost unit, payment in instalments against certificates.

Contract account — debit: materials, wages (including outstanding), direct expenses, plant (or depreciation), overheads; credit: materials returned and in hand, plant at site at closing value, work in progress (certified + uncertified).
Notional profit = value of work done (certified + uncertified) − cost of work done.

Profit on incomplete contracts: less than 25% complete — no profit; 25–50% — 1/3 × notional profit × cash received ÷ work certified; over 50% — 2/3 × notional profit × cash received ÷ work certified; nearly complete — estimated total profit × work certified ÷ contract price. The rest is a reserve. (AS 7 now uses the percentage-of-completion method.)
Work in progress in the Balance Sheet = work certified + uncertified work − profit reserve − cash received.
Contractee's account: debit contract account with work certified; credit cash received — the balance is due.
mistakes: Taking the whole notional profit to P&L on an incomplete contract.
method: Debit all costs; add outstanding wages; debit plant at cost (or charge depreciation).
Credit materials returned, materials and plant at site at year-end.
Credit work certified and uncertified work → balance is notional profit.
Find the stage of completion = work certified ÷ contract price.
Apply the fraction (nil, 1/3 or 2/3) × cash received ÷ work certified → profit to P&L; rest to reserve.
Show WIP in the Balance Sheet net of reserve and cash received.
formula: Notional profit = (Work certified + Uncertified work) − Cost of work done
Profit to P&L (over 50%) = 2/3 × Notional profit × Cash received ÷ Work certified
topics.frame: Contract account in T-form → working note for profit to P&L → WIP in the Balance Sheet.

topics.name: Operating (Service) Costing
topics.summary: Service costing for transport and similar services: cost units, operating cost sheet, cost per km, per passenger-km and per ton-km.
points: Operating or service costing: used by transport, hospitals, hotels, power and water supply; the cost unit is a composite unit such as passenger-km, ton-km, bed-day or kilowatt-hour.

Operating cost sheet: standing (fixed) charges — salaries of staff, garage rent, insurance, taxes, depreciation, interest; maintenance charges — repairs, tyres, servicing; running charges — fuel and oil, drivers' wages (if paid per trip).
Passenger-km = distance × number of passengers carried, where passengers = seats × occupancy %; count both directions and all trips and days.
Ton-km = distance × load carried, including return loads.
mistakes: Counting a round trip as one journey — a round trip is two journeys.
method: List standing, maintenance and running charges for the period (convert annual figures to monthly).
Find total km = distance × 2 (round trip) × trips per day × days × number of vehicles.
Find passenger-km = total km × seats × occupancy % (or ton-km = km × load).
Cost per unit = total operating cost ÷ passenger-km (or ton-km or km).
If a fare is asked, add profit and taxes as instructed.
formula: Passenger-km = Distance × Trips × Days × Vehicles × Seats × Occupancy %
Cost per passenger-km = Total operating cost ÷ Total passenger-km
topics.frame: Operating cost sheet (standing, maintenance, running) → divide by total km, passenger-km or ton-km.

topics.name: Overheads: Classification, Apportionment & Absorption
topics.summary: Concept and classification of overheads, principles and bases of apportionment, primary and secondary distribution, methods of absorption, and under- or over-absorption.
points: Overheads: indirect material, indirect labour and indirect expenses — costs that cannot be traced to a single cost unit.
Classification: by function (factory, office and administration, selling, distribution), by behaviour (fixed, variable, semi-variable), by element, by controllability.

Principles of apportionment: service or use, survey, ability to pay, efficiency. Bases: rent and building costs — floor area; power — horsepower × machine hours; lighting — light points; depreciation and insurance of machines — machine value; canteen and welfare — number of workers; supervision — workers or labour hours.

Primary distribution: spread overheads over production and service departments. Secondary distribution: re-apportion service departments to production departments — direct, step ladder, repeated distribution or simultaneous equations.
Absorption: charging overheads to units — % of direct materials, of direct wages or of prime cost (prime cost method); labour hour rate; machine hour rate; rate per unit.

Under- or over-absorption: causes — wrong estimates, change in capacity used, seasonal effects, method changes, abnormal events. Disposal — supplementary rate, write off to costing P&L, or carry forward if due to a seasonal pattern.

Activity-based costing (ABC): instead of one volume-based rate, costs are traced to the activities that cause them (set-ups, inspections, orders) and charged to products by how much of each activity they use — more accurate where many overheads do not vary with volume.
mistakes: Leaving service department totals unapportioned in the final summary.
method: List each overhead with the basis of apportionment.
Apportion to all departments in the ratio of the basis (primary distribution).
Total each department.
Re-apportion service departments to production departments in the given ratios (secondary distribution).
Divide production department totals by hours or units to get absorption rates if asked.
formula: Overhead absorption rate = Budgeted overheads ÷ Budgeted base (hours, units or % of prime cost)
topics.frame: Overhead distribution summary: columns for each department; one row per overhead with its basis.

units.title: Treatment of Other Overheads and Activity Based Cost Allocation

topics.name: Cost Accounting: Meaning, Objectives & Installation
topics.summary: Meaning, need, objectives and advantages of cost accounting; cost vs financial accounting; limitations of financial accounting; role of the cost accountant; installing a costing system.
points: Cost accounting: classifying, recording and allocating expenses to find the cost of products and services, and presenting the data to management for control and decisions.
Objectives: find the cost of each product, job or process; control and reduce costs; help fix selling prices; value inventory; give information for decisions; measure efficiency.
Advantages: shows profitable and unprofitable products, controls waste, fixes prices, supports budgeting and planning, helps tenders and quotations, compares performance.

Cost vs financial accounting: internal vs external users; product-wise vs overall results; includes estimates and standards vs only actual transactions; optional (mostly) vs compulsory; frequent reports vs annual.
Limitations of financial accounting: historical and overall results only, no product or department costs, no cost control or efficiency measure, no basis for pricing or quotations.

Role of the cost accountant: set up and run the costing system, collect and analyse costs, prepare cost reports and budgets, suggest cost reduction, advise on pricing and decisions, reconcile with financial accounts.

Installing a costing system — points to consider: nature and size of the business, products and processes, organisation, management's needs, a simple and economical system, the right method of costing, forms and records, cooperation of staff, reconciliation with financial accounts. Difficulties: staff resistance, lack of management support, cost of the system, shortage of trained staff — overcome by explaining its benefits, training and starting simply.
topics.frame: Definition → objectives or points as headed list → conclusion.

units.title: Nature and Scope of Cost Accounting

topics.name: Reconciliation of Cost & Financial Accounts
topics.summary: Why profit in cost accounts differs from financial accounts, the reconciliation statement, and integral accounting.
points: Items only in financial accounts: interest and dividends received, profit or loss on sale of assets, rent received, discount on issue of shares, fines, donations, income tax, provisions and appropriations.
Items only in cost accounts: notional charges such as interest on capital or rent on owned premises.
Other causes: under- or over-absorption of overheads, different stock valuations, different depreciation methods, abnormal gains and losses treated differently.

Reconciliation statement: start from profit as per cost accounts; add items that make financial profit higher (over-absorbed overheads, incomes only in financial books, overvaluation of opening stock in cost books…); deduct items that make it lower; the result is profit as per financial accounts.
Integral (integrated) accounting: one set of books for both cost and financial records, so no reconciliation is needed; saves effort and gives quicker, consistent figures.
mistakes: Getting the direction wrong — ask: does this item make financial profit higher or lower than cost profit?
method: Start from the profit in cost accounts (or financial accounts, as asked).
For each item, decide whether it makes financial profit higher or lower.
Add items that increase financial profit; deduct those that reduce it.
Under-absorbed overheads: deduct; over-absorbed: add (starting from cost profit).
Stock: closing stock valued higher in financial books → add; opening stock higher in financial books → deduct.
formula: Profit as per financial accounts = Profit as per cost accounts + Additions − Deductions
topics.frame: Reconciliation statement: Profit as per cost accounts → Add → Less → Profit as per financial accounts.

units.title: Reconciliation of Cost and Financial Accounts

topics.name: Joint Products & By-Products
topics.summary: Joint products and by-products, split-off point, apportionment of joint costs, and accounting for by-products including the reverse cost method.
points: Joint products: two or more products of similar importance from the same process (petrol, diesel and kerosene from crude oil). By-products: products of lower value produced incidentally (molasses from sugar).
Split-off point: the stage at which joint products become separately identifiable.
Apportioning joint costs: physical units, average unit cost, sales value at split-off, net realisable value, technical estimates.

By-products: sales value (less further costs) credited to the main product's process account; or the reverse cost method — sales value minus estimated profit, selling expenses and further processing cost gives the cost credited to the main product.
Treatment depends on value: if negligible, income is credited to costing P&L; if significant, it reduces the main product's cost.
method: Find joint cost up to split-off (materials + labour + overheads).
Reverse cost method: by-product sales − profit − selling costs − further processing = cost to credit.
Credit that amount to the main process account; cost per unit of main product = net cost ÷ output.
For joint products, apportion joint cost in the ratio asked (units or sales value).
formula: By-product cost (reverse method) = Sales value − Profit − Selling and distribution cost − Post-separation cost
topics.frame: Process account for the main product crediting the by-product's value → cost per unit of the main product.

topics.name: Cost Concepts, Classification, Methods & Cost Sheet
topics.summary: Meaning and characteristics of cost, classification of costs, methods of costing and the industries using them, and the cost sheet.
points: Classification: by element (materials, labour, expenses — direct and indirect); by function (production, administration, selling, distribution); by behaviour (fixed, variable, semi-variable); by controllability; by normality; by time (historical, predetermined); for decisions (sunk, opportunity, marginal, differential).

Methods of costing and industries: job (printing, repairs), contract (construction), batch (medicines, toys), process (chemicals, textiles, oil), operating or service (transport, hospitals, power), unit or output (mines, cement, bricks), multiple (cars, radios).

Cost sheet: direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses = prime cost; + factory overheads (± work in progress) = works cost; + office and administration overheads = cost of production; ± finished goods = cost of goods sold; + selling and distribution = cost of sales; + profit = sales.
Unit (output) costing suits a single product made in uniform units (bricks, cement); a cost sheet and a statement of quotation or tender are prepared from it.
method: Prime cost = direct materials consumed (opening stock + purchases − closing stock) + direct wages + direct expenses.
Add factory overheads; adjust opening and closing work in progress → works cost.
Add office and administration overheads → cost of production; adjust finished goods stock.
Add selling and distribution overheads → cost of sales; profit = sales − cost of sales.
Show per-unit figures beside totals when output is given.
formula: Prime cost = Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses
Works cost = Prime cost + Factory overheads + Opening WIP − Closing WIP
Cost of sales = Cost of production ± Finished goods + Selling and distribution overheads
topics.frame: Pro forma cost sheet with headings and imaginary figures.

topics.name: Stock Levels, EOQ & Inventory Control
topics.summary: Reorder, minimum, maximum and danger levels, economic order quantity, ABC analysis, inventory turnover and perpetual inventory.
points: Stock levels keep enough stock to avoid stoppages without overstocking.
ABC analysis: A items — about 10% of items, 70% of value (tight control); B — 20% and 20%; C — 70% of items, 10% of value (simple control).
Inventory turnover ratio = materials consumed ÷ average stock; a high ratio means fast-moving stock; it identifies slow-moving and dead stock and helps cut investment.

Perpetual inventory: a continuous record of receipts, issues and balances in bin cards and the stores ledger, checked by continuous stock-taking — finds losses quickly and gives up-to-date stock figures.
method: Write the given usage and lead-time figures (minimum, normal, maximum).
Reorder level first, then minimum and maximum levels from it.
EOQ: A = annual usage, O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year (price × %).
formula: Reorder level = Maximum usage × Maximum reorder period
Minimum level = Reorder level − (Normal usage × Normal reorder period)
Maximum level = Reorder level + Reorder quantity − (Minimum usage × Minimum reorder period)
EOQ = √(2 × A × O ÷ C)
Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of materials consumed ÷ Average stock

topics.name: Machine Hour Rate
topics.summary: Computing a machine hour rate from standing charges and machine expenses.
points: Machine hour rate: the overhead cost of running a machine for one hour, used to absorb overheads where machines do most of the work.
Standing (fixed) charges: rent, lighting, supervisor's salary, insurance — shared by the machine's share of area or time; spread over the machine's working hours.
Machine expenses (variable): depreciation, power, repairs, consumables — worked out per hour directly.
Depreciation per hour = (cost + installation − scrap value) ÷ total working hours in the machine's life.
mistakes: Charging all rent or the whole supervisor's salary to one machine — use its share.
method: Find working hours per period (month or year).
Standing charges for the machine's share (area, time) for the period ÷ working hours = standing charges per hour.
Depreciation per hour = (cost + installation − scrap) ÷ life hours.
Power per hour = units per hour × rate per unit; repairs and consumables ÷ hours.
Machine hour rate = standing charges per hour + machine expenses per hour.
formula: Machine hour rate = Standing charges per hour + Machine expenses per hour
Depreciation per hour = (Cost + Installation − Scrap value) ÷ Life in hours
topics.frame: Table: standing charges per period → per hour; machine expenses per hour → total rate per hour.
